"Jacked" is an informal, slang adjective. It has a few different meanings, and the right one always depends on context. Here is every meaning you need to know, explained fully.

This is the dominant modern meaning. If someone is jacked, they have an exceptionally muscular, well-built body — the kind that comes from serious, dedicated weightlifting or intense physical training. It's not just "fit" or "strong." It specifically suggests large, visibly defined muscles that are hard to miss.

Think of it on a scale:
Thin → Average → Fit → Strong → Muscular → Jacked

"Jacked" sits at the far end. It implies an impressive, almost striking level of muscularity.

Examples:

  • "He trains twice a day. The guy is absolutely jacked."
  • "She's been lifting for three years — she's seriously jacked."
  • "You can tell he used to play football. Still jacked."

"Jacked" can describe a person who is intensely excited, pumped up, or energized — usually about something that is about to happen. It captures that buzzing, restless, can't-wait feeling.

Examples:

  • "I'm so jacked for this trip. I've been waiting months."
  • "The whole locker room was jacked before the championship game."

This meaning is less common than Meaning 1, but it is widely understood.

In certain informal and urban American speech, "jacked" means something was stolen, often forcefully or boldly. You'll usually hear this in the form "got jacked."

Examples:

  • "My bike got jacked right outside my apartment."
  • "Someone jacked his phone on the train."

This meaning is more regionally common (particularly in the US) and is not universally used everywhere English is spoken.
Meaning 4: "Jacked Up" — A Closely Related Phrase

When you combine "jacked" with "up," you get the phrase "jacked up," which functions as its own adjective and carries a separate set of meanings. Since learners frequently encounter it alongside "jacked," you need to know it.

a) Messed Up, Broken, or Wrong

This is probably the most common use of "jacked up." It describes something that is in bad shape, dysfunctional, unfair, or just plain wrong. It can apply to physical things, situations, systems, or behavior.

  • "The whole project got jacked up when the files were deleted."
  • "That's jacked up." (= That's messed up / That's not right)
  • "My knee has been jacked up since the accident."

b) Wired or Over-Stimulated

Describing a person who is hyper or unusually energized — typically from caffeine, sugar, or stimulants.

  • "She had four coffees and was completely jacked up."
  • "The kids were jacked up on Halloween candy."

c) Inflated / Raised Unreasonably (Prices or Amounts)

When prices, fees, or numbers have been pushed much higher than they should be.

  • "The prices at the airport are totally jacked up."
  • "They jacked up the rent by 40%."

d) Physically Raised (Literal)

Describing something that has been physically lifted — often a vehicle lifted with a car jack. This is the most literal use of the phrase.

  • "The car was jacked up on a lift while the mechanic changed the tires."
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

Since the word has multiple meanings, here is how context guides you:

  • Describing a person's body → muscular
  • Describing a person's emotions before an event → excited
  • Describing something stolen → stolen
  • "Jacked up" + a situation, system, or behavior → messed up or wrong
  • "Jacked up" + a person on caffeine or stimulants → wired/hyper
  • "Jacked up" + prices or numbers → inflated
  • "Jacked up" + a physical object being lifted → raised
Register: How Formal Is This Word?

"Jacked" in all of its forms is informal slang. It is perfectly natural and widely used in everyday conversation, text messages, social media, and casual speech. You would not use it in formal writing, professional emails, or academic work. In those settings, you would replace it with:

  • Jacked (body) → muscular, well-built
  • Jacked (excited) → enthusiastic, eager
  • Jacked (stolen) → stolen, taken
  • Jacked up (messed up) → dysfunctional, flawed, unjust
  • Jacked up (prices) → inflated, exorbitant

In summary, the word "jacked" is mostly about muscles in everyday use, but it branches into excitement, theft, and dysfunction depending on how it's used. The key is always context — once you know the situation being described, the meaning becomes obvious.
